utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you call case number, Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic, and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Tecla Henry-Benjamin, Daryl Mundis, and the case manager Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. And could we have the appearances for the Defence, who are not all present.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of the General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, lead counsel; and Alexis Demirdjian, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present in the courtroom, members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, and everyone else present in the courtroom as well as the interpreters who are outside the courtroom. Today we will continue with the examination of a witness. Before we call the witness into the courtroom, there is a minor clarification I would like to provide you with concerning the -- our future work. Tomorrow is the beginning of July. We have a number of witnesses who still have to be called. I would like to inform the Prosecution that they will have up until Friday, the 23rd. That will be the last day on which we will be able to have a hearing, because after that date the Trial Chamber will be occupied with the Tribunal's Plenary Sessions, and then we will have the holiday period in August. So after the 23rd of July, the first hearing that we could have would be on the 31st of August, Monday, the 31st of August. In July there are also two days when the Trial Chamber won't be sitting. That will be on the 19th and the 20th of July. So the Prosecution should bear this in mind when planning its case. And the end of its case, the Prosecution's case, should have been at the beginning of June, but given the particular circumstances that arose, we have not yet concluded this stage of the proceedings. So in summary, we have 23 days, but Friday the 23rd will have to be the last day. And on the 19th and 20th of July, we won't be having a hearing. We will resume on Wednesday, the 21st. And if there is a witness who is not available for 15 days, I think that might cause a problem. Mr. Mundis, as far as this schedule is concerned, are there any comments you would like to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As the Trial Chamber is well aware, we -- we do have just a small number of witnesses, but as Your Honour has indicated, one of those witnesses is unavailable for approximately 15 days. VWS is in the process of attempting to communicate with the other witness. We will, of course, ensure that we comply with the Trial Chamber's Scheduling Order as just indicated. At some point it would, I think, be of assistance to both parties to at least get some preliminary thoughts from the Trial Chamber as to scheduling with respect to 98 bis submissions. Of course the time frame for those, pursuant to the Rules, runs from the completion of the Prosecution case. However, it might be of some assistance at some point if we could get some preliminary thoughts after, of course, hearing from the Defence, as to the timetable in which the Trial Chamber might be expecting the parties to file their written submissions pursuant to that Rule. Other than that, Mr. President, the schedule as set forth is certainly manageable from the Prosecution point of view, assuming that we get the documents all sorted and the remaining witnesses are made available. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I will give the floor to the Defence to hear what their comments are. According to the schedule I have just mentioned, as I said, the last day on which we could have a hearing would be the 23rd of July. 98 bis can only enter into force at the end of the Prosecution's case. So if I extrapolate from what you said, you said that the witness who should be here in 15 days' time should enable you to finish by the 23rd of July, at the latest. Is that correct, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We anticipate no problems with that schedule, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm now addressing the Defence. You've heard what has just been said. The Prosecution would like to have certain clarifications with regard to Rule 98 bis, because as you are well aware, once the Prosecution has officially stated that they have completed the presentation of their case, you have seven days, and if necessary, you can be granted additional time. So it would be useful if you could tell us at this point in time whether you have already given any thought to the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. And I'd like to thank the Trial Chamber for having indicated certain dates when it will be possible to work, and the Plenary Session. It's quite clear to us that after the Prosecution has concluded the presentation of its case, it is then time for us to prepare for the entry into force of Rule 98 bis. As far as I have understood my colleagues from the Prosecution, they stated before the Trial Chamber that their case should be concluded not only once they have completed the examinations of the witnesses but also once the Trial Chamber's decision on the admissibility of documents has been rendered. So it is obvious that today we can't say when the exact date would be as far as submissions or filing of submission is concerned. Naturally we will take advantage of our right according to the Rules. It's at least eight days after the decision has been rendered on the conclusion of the Prosecution's case, but according to the practice followed before this Chamber, even in simpler cases the Defence is given three weeks, and we believe that the Trial Chamber will understand that this is the minimum period the Defence requires in order to file its motion. I also think that the Chamber will give the Prosecution an opportunity to respond to our motion. If the Trial Chamber could take into consideration the fact that August is a holiday period, not only for all those who work in the Tribunal but also -- and for us who will be dealing with the defence, but it's also a holiday period for the people working for us or the witnesses whom we have to contact during that period. As a result, when the Trial Chamber presents its plan, could they take into consideration the fact that the Defence counsel will not be in a position to work effectively for a one-month period, and could we be allowed to have sufficient time to prepare? According to the practice followed before the Tribunal, after submissions are filed, the Trial Chamber usually lets the Defence have two or three weeks to prepare in order to present its case. That's when the Defence case commences with its opening statement. We have discussed this subject. We don't have any specific suggestions, but we do believe that the Trial Chamber, when giving thought to the proceedings that will be followed -- the procedure that will be followed by the Defence and by the Prosecution, we believe that the Trial Chamber will take into consideration the suggestions and submissions that we have made today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your submissions. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have nothing other to add to what Mrs. Residovic has just stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the Defence counsel have said that after the Prosecution has concluded the presentation of its case, it believes that, in conformity with the practice followed here, they should be granted at least three weeks to make their submissions, file their motions. The Defence counsel has also stated that this is something that will occur during the so-called court recess, during the holiday period, and this is something that should be borne in mind. It is also obvious that once the submissions have been made, once the motions have been filed, the Prosecution will have a certain period of time, usually the same period of time, so that the Prosecution can respond. So if I add this up very rapidly, three weeks plus three weeks means that we would -- that it would take us up to mid-September more or less. The Judges will discuss the matter, and we will then provide you with a schedule for the future, but for the moment we have taken note of what you have said and your positions. The positions you have stated have been very reasonable. Mr. Mundis, in view of what the Defence has just said, is there anything you would like to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have nothing to add at this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What is important, naturally, is to know when you will have concluded the presentation of your case. It's important to know the exact date, and that's when we will decide on when time should start running for the Defence, but we know that you have plans to make, things that you have to organise, so this is something that will be addressed later. I think that Mr. Bourgon wanted to say something about the documents. That's the impression I had yesterday, but he is not here, so you won't be making any submissions. Mr. Bourgon said that he would be making some submissions, but he is not present here. So if he hasn't given you any instructions, any information --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you know, this is Mr. Bourgon's responsibility. That's how we have divided our tasks. So if he thinks it is necessary, he will address the Trial Chamber tomorrow. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's with great pleasure that we have heard that he will be here tomorrow and we will give him the floor so that he can make the submissions he wants to make. If there are no other issues to raise by either of the parties, I will now ask the usher to bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I -- if I could, while the witness is being brought in, again for the record as the Prosecution has previously indicated, this witness we expect will be a Defence witness and consequently the questioning put to this witness by the Prosecution will be limited to one of the specific points pursuant to the Trial Chamber's 17 May 2004 oral order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I would like to make sure that you are receiving interpretation of what I'm saying. If so, please say that you are receiving the interpretation and that you can understand everything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hear in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He can hear what I'm saying in English. Can you hear what is being said in English? I wanted to say that you have been called here as a witness by the Prosecution. I will get back to that in a minute, but as you've been called to testify, you have to take the solemn declaration. Before you do so, could you please give me your first and last names, could you tell me your date of birth and your place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Senad Selimovic. I was born on the 30th of December, 1956, in Zenica in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What duties do you perform at the moment or what is your current position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a pensioner now, and I'm a former member of the BH Federation army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're a member of the military as retired. What was the rank you held before you retired and when did you retire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a brigadier in the Federation army, and I retired on the 30th of May, 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Brigadier. Would that be an officer's rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's the highest rank an officer can have in the Federation army. It's above the rank of general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So should one call you "General"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shouldn't call you "General." The rank below that of general in all the armies throughout the world is that of a colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To tell you the truth, I don't know why that is the case. That is the rank in certain armies. In other armies that's the rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The witness said that the rank above that of brigadier is general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will ask you, Colonel -- I will call you Colonel. That will be a lot simpler. When you went into retirement, which unit were you in just before you went into retirement in the year 2004?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a member of the Joint Command of the Federation army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And my last question before you take the solemn declaration. In 1993, were you a member of the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which unit were you a member of and what rank did you hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a member of the 3rd Corps of the BH army. I had the rank that I had in the former JNA, the rank of captain first class.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, sir. In 1993, you were a captain. Have you already testified before an international or national court with regard to the events that took place in Bosnia in 1993 or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, as I have already said, you have been called here as a witness by the Prosecution. You have been called here to testify because the Trial Chamber has to resolve an issue that concerns certain documents. Your presence here has to do with certain technical issues that relate to documents. In the course of previous hearings, we found out that you were supposed to be a witness for the Defence, and it is only recently that we Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. discovered that you were a Defence witness, whereas you have now been called by the Prosecution. So all you will have to do now is answer technical questions that have to do with the documents. We won't be talking about any other issues of substance. The Prosecution will be putting questions to you. Once they have put their questions to you -- the Prosecution are to your right and you met them awhile ago in your country. Once they have put the questions to you, Defence counsel, who are to your left, will conduct what we call their cross-examination. If necessary, the Prosecution will take the floor again to put additional questions to you. The three Judges sitting before you will also ask you questions that relate to technical issues, relate to the transmission of documents, et cetera, et cetera. Perhaps we won't have so many questions to ask you, but when we do ask you questions, this will be to clarify certain answers you have provided or because the Judges believe that there are certain gaps that should be filled and certain issues that should be clarified. You've taken the solemn declaration. If you give false testimony -- if one gives false testimony, one could be prosecuted. And there is something else I would like to inform you of, but this shouldn't be applicable to you: A witness may refuse to answer questions that could incriminate the witness. In such a case, the Trial Chamber can compel the witness to answer, but the witness is granted a form of immunity. Try to answer the questions as precisely and clearly as possible. That is, you are an officer, you know what that means. It's necessary for your answer to be sufficiently clear for us to understand, because if we don't understand your answer, then there's no point in putting questions to you. That's why your testimony is so important. If you fail to understand a question, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it. If you encounter difficulties of any kind, do tell us. You're here to testify about purely technical matters, so you should be relaxed, and you shouldn't be concerned by the questions that will be put to you. I am now turning to Mr. Mundis, who will take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Selimovic. You told the Trial Chamber in response to one of the preliminary questions that you had been in the JNA. Can you please tell us when you first joined the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: I joined the Yugoslav People's Army in June 1978, when I graduated from the Military Air Force Academy in Rajlovac, near Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And upon graduating from the Military Air Force Academy, what subsequent training or specialisation, specialised training, did you receive?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: In the JNA, after graduation and after I began working at the Bihac airport to which I was assigned, I mainly attended these military courses intended for advanced training. The first course I completed was as a commander of a communications company, a course for commanders of communication companies. But nothing more than that in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the branch or specialised branch of the JNA air force that you served in?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: I was promoted to the position of communications officer so that throughout I was mainly active in that area. That is the branch of the army that deals with communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, when you say "throughout," what time period or for what period of time were you a communications specialist?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: From -- at the beginning, I was commander of a communications platoon, then a communications company, then in Bihac there was at the level of the brigade. Those were the duties I performed for the JNA. As for the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I performed the duties of the head of communications for the district staff in Zenica up until the formation of the 3rd Corps. When the 3rd Corps was formed, I became head of communications for the 3rd Corps as assistant chief of staff for communications. And after the war, I was appointed to the position of deputy assistant chief of staff for telecommunications in the Joint Command of the army of the Federation. That was the duty that I performed until my retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So based on this answer, Mr. Selimovic, would it be fair to say that for more than a quarter century you were involved in military communications?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me just go back and ask you to elaborate briefly on your answer of a few moments ago. You told us that in Bihac, while serving with the JNA air force, you commanded a brigade, a communications brigade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, I was commander of the communications company at Bihac airport, which is an air force base. And for those who don't know, this is the equivalent to a brigade. And at the same time, I was chief of communications in the brigade. So I had those two positions. I was commander of the communications company, and at the same time head of communications for the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us approximately when you left the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: In April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Following your departure from the JNA, what military did you immediately serve in, or what force did you immediately serve in after leaving the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: With my children, I went to Zenica. This was in April 1992. And then after that, I couldn't return to Bihac, where I had lived until then, and on the 30th of April I reported to the district staff of the defence of Zenica, of the Territorial Defence. So the district staff of the Territorial Defence of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, just for the record, you told us that you reported there on 30 April. Can you tell us what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long did you remain with the district staff of the Territorial Defence of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Until the establishment of the command of the 3rd Corps. Simply as soon as the 3rd Corps was established, I was appointed to head of communications of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, while you remained from the 30th of April, 1992, until the establishment of the 3rd Corps, during the time period you were with the district staff of the Territorial Defence of Zenica, what were your duties and responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: In the district staff, I was appointed to the position of chief of communications of the district staff of the Territorial Defence of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Selimovic, do you recall approximately when the 3rd Corps was established?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: In November 19 -- end of November 1992. Yes, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you told us, sir, that your duties there were as assistant -- assistant staff -- can you tell us again your precise title with the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: In the staff, I was appointed to the position assistant chief of staff for communications. Actually, it was the position of chief of communications of the 3rd Corps. These positions are frequently given different names, but actually they're one and the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And based on this position, would it be fair to characterise you as being the chief of communications or the most senior communications officer within the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber how long you remained with the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: I remained in the 3rd Corps actually until the end of the war. And in 1997, I think, I became a member of the Joint Command of the Federation army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And throughout the period of time from the establishment of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 3rd Corps, when you were attached to that unit until you detached from that unit sometime after the war, did you remain in the post of chief of communications?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us the -- to whom you reported as the chief of communications. Who was your immediate supervisor?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: In the 3rd Corps, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: My superior was Mekic Muradif, chief of staff in the command of the 3rd Corps, my immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long was Mekic Muradif your supervisor as the chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly now, but for as long as he was chief of staff. I can't give you the exact date. I think it was the end of 1992, which would mean from November until, shall we say, mid-1993 maybe. Maybe even into the autumn. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I take it then, sir, based on these answers that you've given us, that as the chief of communications you reported directly to the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, most often.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us, then, the chain of command upwards from the chief of staff within the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: If I may, I would like to say that the commander of the 3rd Corps was General Hadzihasanovic. His deputy -- there was the position of Deputy Commander in those days, and General Dzemal Merdan was appointed to that position, and I think that the number three man in the hierarchy was Muradif Mekic. Actually, this position of deputy commander existed in some units and others it didn't. In units in which there was no deputy commander, then the chief of staff was the second in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But just so that we're clear, in the 3rd Corps, there was at the top the commander, followed by the deputy commander, followed by the chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber a little bit about what your responsibilities entailed as the communications officer for the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: This communications section within the staff was an administration and planning body engaged in the planning and organisation of communications in the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about what you mean by "planning and organisation of communications"? What exactly does that mean?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: I would be the specialised body of the chief of staff who was the highest person responsible for the system of communications and its planning and organisation, that is of the communications system within the command of the 3rd Corps. And an administrative planning body, when I say that, it means that I didn't have the ability to issue orders. I was a consultative body, somebody who would propose the organisation of the system of communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us that you didn't have the ability to issue orders. Are you familiar in any sense of how orders or regulations that would govern orders, what regulations were in effect?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, a certain organisational process was applied when decisions were made. Sometimes the process would take time, sometimes it was quite brief, and sometimes the commander himself would make the decisions. And I would take part, as the chief of communications, in drafting orders with respect to communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me -- let me take a step backwards. I'll ask you a little bit more about these issues in just a moment. Were there regulations in force that governed how to draft orders and what orders should look like and the formatting of orders and these types of issues?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: We applied what we knew on the basis of our professional experience from the past. We used certain instructions from the former JNA which regulated the format of orders and what they should contain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So there was some type of set template or format for what orders should look like. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned to us a little bit about how orders actually came to be drafted. Can you tell us how -- in some detail how that actually worked in practice. How were orders actually drafted?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: The orders were drafted in different ways, ranging from an individual or a specialist in a particular area. If the order related to that area only, he would prepare the possible text of the order. And then also this could be done during an organisational process, in a summary proceeding, or when several participants would contribute elements or parts to that order. And also there were cases where the commander himself or one of his deputies or the chief of staff could draft the order themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd like you to be as precise as possible, Witness, with respect to the issue of who had the authority to issue the order.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, the commander of the 3rd Corps, General Hadzihasanovic. Also, up to a point, the deputy commander, General Dzemal Merdan, and the chief of staff, Mr. Muradif Mekic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You've told us about the process whereby a number of individuals might be involved in drafting the orders. Would those individuals be doing that at their own initiative or would they be following specific instructions from the senior leadership of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: In most cases there would be instructions from the superiors. In most cases on the whole, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us about specific instances where an officer or a staff officer might draft an order on his or her own initiative?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, occasionally there would be a situation when only that particular area was affected, and then orders might be issued that were of lesser importance. When something needed to be regulated and the superiors were not there, who were frequently in the field or at advance command posts or touring the units, and then what might happen would be for such orders to be written in their absence. Or a superior might give instructions to someone to prepare an order for a particular unit for the particular area for which he is the expert, because the commander and chief of staff couldn't be familiar with all the details, so they most frequently consulted their subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Who had the authority to sign written orders for the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recollect, as far as I know and to the best of my knowledge, it was the commander, the deputy commander, and the chief of staff. Those are the three persons who had that authority. Sometimes - I can't say exactly when - there would be case when an officer from the operations department who would sometimes be, shall we say, the number four in rank, and possibly also from the special branches or services, an order of lesser importance, one that didn't affect everyone, so maybe the best term to use might be the orders of lesser importance might be signed by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you've told us that the deputy commander or the chief of staff or some of these other officers could sign orders. Would they sign orders if the commander were present? Would those individuals be the one issuing orders if the commander was present at the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think not. In writing, no. Certainly if the commander is there, then he was the one to do it mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So if we're clear, then the commander would sign the orders if he was present; but if he was not present, then who would sign?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: In most cases, these two other persons; that is, the deputy commander, General Merdan, and the chief of staff, Muradif Mekic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And if General Merdan was present but General Hadzihasanovic was not, would the chief of staff sign the documents?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've already told you that that position was questionable. Actually, we weren't sure whether the deputy was number two or the chief of staff was number two, and even later on a clear distinction couldn't be made. But in any case, both of them would sign if the commander was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. absent, or if two of the three were absent. There were such situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what about situations where all three of them were absent? Who would sign orders for the 3rd Corps in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: In exceptional cases, but rather rarely, it would be the operations officer, or the head of the operations department, the chief of the operations department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, sir, were there any standing orders within the 3rd Corps setting forth who could sign documents when the senior leaders were absent?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember actually seeing such standing orders, but it was a kind of unwritten rule that I remember such, that it was the persons who held these positions who had the authority to sign orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, that would in fact follow from common military sense and training, would it not, that there is always someone in charge, even in the absence of the commander, deputy, chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, let me turn now to the issue of the preparation, if you will, the physical preparation of written orders. You've already told us that in some instances there might be a collaborative process or a number of individuals might be involved in writing an order, but how would that be done? How would they write an order?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in brief, the commander would have and set forth his idea as to what the contents of the document should be, of the order, and then the specialised bodies, the assistants, and senior officers in the staff would actually start the process, and they would finally propose points in the order relating to the specific areas that the order was meant to cover, upon which the commander would accept or reject these proposals made by his assistants or the assistants of the chief of staff with respect to their specific areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were these orders written by hand or were they typed on a typewriter or a computer? How were they actually physically produced, the written orders?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, the orders were mostly written on a typewriter, and then later on a computer would be used. Actually, in most cases it was a PC, so that mostly all the orders, at least in the 3rd Corps Command, were done on a computer, afterwards printed out by a printer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what would happen to the document that was printed out after it came out of the printer? What would be the process?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: It would be carried to the commander for him to sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And once the commander signed the document, the order, what would happen then?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Then the order would go to the administrative department of the staff, where it would be registered and certified with a stamp, that is to certify the commander's signature or the signature of whoever it was that had signed the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about what you mean by "certifying." What was the process about? How was it done?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: The first certification is the signature itself of the person who signed the document. In this case, it would be the commander, his deputy, or chief of staff. After that, a stamp was used, a round stamp specific to the unit, whereby the authenticity of the signature is certified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Who did the certifying?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mainly the -- in the administrative department, the staff in that department. That may have consisted of three or four men who would take turns working there. Anyway, that was their responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how would they actually determine the authenticity of the signature prior to placing the stamp on the order?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: They had to know what the signature looked like, the signature of the commander or the person who has the right to sign. I think they would know more about that, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know how -- you told us they, the administrative officer, had to know what the signature looked like. Do you have any information or knowledge as to how they would know what the signature looked like?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that they -- the person who has the authority to sign and his signature to be stamped has to deposit that signature. I'm not sure that we implemented that rule at the time, but probably that was how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So I take it from that answer, then, that when you say deposit the signature, there would be some kind of a list of these authorised signatures and the administrative officer would compare that and then certificate it and stamp it?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think so, yes. I think that's how it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Once the written order was then signed, certified, and stamped, what would be done with the written order?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that communications had been planned, in those days we had planned radio communications, some wire communications, courier communications, the way would be defined how the document would be carried. In most cases it was by courier because the communications system could not send off documents that were lengthy, that consisted of several pages. So brief orders went through communications links, documents that were one to two pages long at the outside, but in most cases the orders would be carried by courier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were the orders that were carried by the couriers, did they all have original signatures and original stamps, or did the original signed copy remain with the 3rd Corps headquarters?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, different procedures were followed at times, but on the whole, these documents were documents that had all been signed, all copies of these documents had been signed by the commander and then this circular stamp was placed on the document. Sometimes, for the sake of procedure, in order to be rapid, the commander would only sign one original document, which would remain in the archives, and then the document would be copied, the document with his signature, and then that copy would be stamped and perhaps there would be something mentioning that the copy had been made on the basis of an authentic document issued by the commander. So two procedures were followed. A copy of the commander's signature could be stamped, so to speak, but there would be an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a few follow-on questions based on -- on what you've just told us. I take it from the answer that in some circumstances or in some situations multiple copies of an order, such as an order to all units, multiple copies might be printed out and all of those signed by the commander and certified and stamped?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were cases when this procedure was followed, but as I said, there were also cases in which there was only one document, one order that was signed, and then copies of that document with the commander's signature would be made. The copy would then be stamped, and this was confirmation that the document was an authentic one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So just so that we're clear, sir, the -- if the document were to be photocopied or somehow copied after the commander signed it, it would still get a stamp on it to certify that the photocopy was an accurate copy of the original before it was then sent out to the unit it was addressed to?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what was most frequently done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What colour or colours were used by the administrative staff to stamp documents?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Usually the colour used was blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you've also told us, sir, that the document, after it was sent, or -- let me rephrase the question. Was an original or was the original copy of the order retained at the 3rd Corps headquarters?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Usually, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what would happen to that original? Where was it kept? How were they maintained?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: That was usually kept in the archives. It was changed at different times, but it was usually kept in the archives. That's the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. document that would be kept by the person who had drafted the order, by the person who had processed it. Sometimes it was the commander, and sometimes, as I said, it was the deputy, sometimes it was the chief of staff. These people might have the document, but it was kept in a so-called archive. So it wasn't in fact a real archives, but that's more or less how the documents were kept or stored in the archives. Or let's say it would be in the administration department that was in charge of those archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So the 3rd Corps administrative department maintained an archive of the original documents?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Usually, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I neglected to ask you one question earlier when we were talking about individuals other than the commander signing the original document. Can you tell us the typewritten or computer written signature block on 3rd Corps documents, whose name would appear on documents issued by the 3rd Corps, the typewritten or computer written name at the bottom of the order?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Usually the first and last name of the 3rd Corps commander, General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about those instances where someone other than General Hadzihasanovic signed the document? Whose typewritten name would appear? Would it still be the commander's, or who it be the individual who actually signed the order?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Usually in most of the cases there would be the first and last name of the commander, General Hadzihasanovic. His name was always printed out at the bottom. The document was ready to be signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In the event someone other than the commander signed the document, such as the deputy commander or chief of staff or someone from the operations department, if they signed the document, would there be any indication on the document that someone other than the commander was signing the document?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes there would be the handwritten word "for," which meant the deputy, and then there would be the signature of that person. You'd have the printed name of General Hadzihasanovic, and it would be signed by one of these two or three persons. Sometimes there was the word "for," and sometimes the word "for" wasn't contained on the document and then you would have the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So what you're telling us, sir, is that the word "for" might not appear on all the documents when someone other than the commander signed it?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what would happen. That's what the documents looked like, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, for the benefit of those of us who unfortunately don't speak the Bosnian language, can you spell the word "for" in Bosnian for the transcript?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Z-a. Z-a.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Selimovic. Let me turn now to the issue of the transmission of written orders to the field. You've already told us that in general if a document was lengthy it would be sent by courier, but if it was a shorter document, it would be sent by other means. Let me ask you in general about what communications means were available to the 3rd Corps for the transmission of written orders during the period 1993.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: As I have already said, radio communications were used, wire communications, and courier -- couriers were used. That was the plan. We had communications means. When I say radio communications, I'm thinking of HF, high frequency, communications, and VVF -- VHF, very high frequency radio links. These -- the high frequency means were amateur devices at the time in the course of 1993, and VHF -- the VF equipment was used for long distances, and the VHF shorter distances. We also used equipment devices from the former JNA. It was very difficult for us to maintain these devices, this equipment, owing to the lack of spare parts and cuts in electricity supplies -- supply. This was old equipment. Then we used wire communications between units. We used the communication means of the post office. Their equipment hadn't been destroyed when the fighting first broke out. This was the case in territory where we could use such equipment. And as I said, we also used couriers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, sir, let me ask you some follow-on questions based on that answer. Can you tell us how an HF or VHF radio system would be used to transmit written orders?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Speeches were forwarded through the system, the spoken word was transmitted through this system, but later we obtained certain modems, radio modems, and with that device they were linked up to a computer. And then information would be noted at one point, we'd have the computer, the modem, and the radio device, and this would then be relayed to a second point which also consisted of a modem/computer set-up. So we used the adequate communications programmes and also cryptographic programmes that made it possible for written documents to be forwarded to another point in written form, in the form in which the document had been issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit more about the wire communication systems? What kind of systems were those, and what were the names of any of such systems?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, to an extent, we used this means with the brigade in Kakanj, the units in Kakanj. I know that wire link functioned there, and again we used a similar system: There was a telephone linked to a telephone modem and a computer. This was the set-up at one point. And the second point we'd have the same set-up, if it was at our disposal, and again it was again possible to relay written information between those two points, as is the case today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you also mentioned using the communication means of the post office. Can you tell us a little bit more about what you meant when you said that?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: That system was destroyed in the course of the conflict. So parts of the system were used. In some places there was an automatic telephone exchange that was operational, and we used those means in order to phone. This was mostly locally, between those individual towns. For example, as far as Kakanj, this was a system that functioned. We had lines consisting of two wires similar to telephone lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with a system known as the Paket or package system?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did the 3rd Corps have the Paket or package system; and if so, when was that first available to the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's a system that was developed on VHF radio links. That was a form of communication developed by amateurs, radio amateurs, and it made it possible to send written information, and we started organising such a system. The 3rd Corps did have this system, but naturally it was being developed with all units. It started at the beginning of 1993, and as time passed by, this system was used more and more frequently, because as I said, it's necessary to have two points to maintain such a link-up. You need two set-ups between two units. It wasn't always possible to have such a set-up on the other side, at the other point, but the command in the 3rd Corps did have Paket communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I take it when you say it started at the beginning of 1993, that over the course of some period of time, the Paket system became widely used by the subordinate units of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But as I have said, this is a system that took us a lot of time to develop because we didn't have a sufficient number of computers. We didn't have enough equipment. We didn't have enough modems. There was the blockade, and finally these modems arrived from Croatia through certain channels. The system was limited as a result of lack of resources, and it was further limited because of personnel problems. We had to train people on one side, then this training had to be provided to the other side. So we needed all these elements, all these material Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. elements, for it to function. There were links between the corps command and individual units, and later on this developed into a real system which did function if, as I said, all the other means had been provided, because this system was quite frequently obstructed since the other side used a similar system and knew how to obstruct it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about what the document, the order, looked like when it came out on the other end of the Paket system, at the receiving end. The unit receiving an order via the Paket system, how did that order look different than the original order that was maintained at the headquarters in the archive?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was different in that it wasn't possible to relay the signature to the other side. We couldn't send the electronic signature of the person who had signed the original document. So the contents of the document were identical at the other side, but there was no stamp and no signature. All we had was the typewritten name, for example, of the 3rd Corps commander, General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So, sir, I take it from that answer, then, that the Paket system was not like - was not like - fax technology where you scan a document in and the document comes out the other end with signatures, characters, stamps, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, it's different. There's no signature, no stamp. It's just the electronic part that is relayed. All you have is what the computer recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And if you can, sir, briefly, because we're almost up to our technical break, can you tell us a little bit about how that written order that had been certified, signed, stamped, et cetera, how was that written order entered into the Paket system for transmission to subordinate units in the field? How was this done since it wasn't scanned into the computer or system?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: At first, as I said, the documents were typed out on typewriters, and the document would be signed and certified, and if it had to be relayed by the communications system, it would go through the administration department to the corps command. There was a computer in the communications centre -- once we had developed the Paket system, there was a computer linked up to a modem, and sometimes there was a radio or a modem, and such a document as an authentic document with a stamp and signature would arrive in the centre. First of all, it would be typed out again, but this system was soon changed and a computer was used. So an electronic record would arrive on a disk, it would arrive in the centre, and also original document with the stamp and a signature. And the official in the communications centre who dealt with these matters, once he opened a file on the computer, would check the authenticity. He would compare the document to the original, and the document would then be forwarded. It would be encrypted and sent to its destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I have just a couple of follow-up questions and then we'll take our technical break. The first one is, just so that we're clear, there were really two systems or two ways the written order could be sent via Paket: It could either be retyped in by the administrative officer who had the original signed, certified copy in front of him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: This is something that was done in the communications centre. As you say, the document would be retyped, but we soon got a second computer which made it possible for the document to be processed immediately so it was not necessary to retype it as this took up a lot of time. So we accelerated the process. The document was then processed on the computer, and a disk would be used to take it to the communications centre, and the centre was then able to forward the document more rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But, sir, under either of those two approaches, whether it was retyped or whether it was used or transmitted from a disk, the person actually sending the order via the Paket system would confirm the contents of the electronic order with the signed, certified, and stamped original prior to sending it.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I note the time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You will continue a short while later. Is it your intention to show the witness documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have two or perhaps three additional areas to cover in the examination and then our intention was - and I notified the Defence of this this morning - was to show the witness four of the original contested documents and ask him to comment briefly on those documents. Obviously, document handling can take a little bit of time. I'm -- I will endeavour to finish within 30 minutes, but I may not make it quite within 30 minutes. I do have copies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Do you have the numbers of the documents that you will be presenting?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I do, and I also have copies. If I -- if that would be easier for the Chamber, I can hand out the copies now. I have provided copies to both of the Defence teams as well as to both of the accused, but I certainly have sufficient copies that I can make available now for Your Honours. There are, as I said, four documents. There are numerous copies there, and I'll take whatever is remaining after the usher has handed them out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I put this question to you so that the Chamber's legal officer can find the originals that should be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just, to short circuit this, I signed out from the legal officer custody of a number of documents yesterday. The documents I'll be showing the witness, I have physical custody of the originals and they were the ones that I signed out yesterday, so I have the original documents with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you will be showing the witness the originals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now adjourn, and we will resume at about 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Immediately before the break, Mr. Selimovic, we were talking about how orders were actually transmitted to units in the field, and I'd like to pick up on a related issue. Once the document, the order, the written order, was sent to a subordinate unit or units, you told us the original was kept at the 3rd Corps headquarters; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, what markings, if any, would have been made on the original to indicate that it was actually sent or transmitted?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: It depended on the way it was sent. If it went by courier -- if it went by courier, then somebody would sign in the -- at the destination that he had received such an order. If the communications devices were used on the original, a rectangular stamp would be affixed indicating when the message was sent and received and the hour when it was sent to the other unit. This stamp contained several pieces of information as evidence that something had been sent at a certain time, and on the other hand that it was also received at a certain point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay, sir. I'd like you to focus -- I'll ask you a little bit about the documents being received, but I'm specifically talking about documents being sent from the 3rd Corps headquarters. These markings that you've told us about, did those apply to documents being sent, a stamp and/or a signature indicating that it was sent?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, if the documents were being sent by courier. But if a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. communications system was used, at the other end, for technical reasons, the signature could not be received. That is, the stamp could not be transmitted. So it wasn't the same system as faxes but only the written text that was typed out on the computer could be transmitted in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me try to go about this a slightly different way just to make sure we're all clear. When an order was sent by courier, what indication, if any, would be made on the original order maintained in the headquarters to demonstrate that the order was sent out by courier?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: In most cases it would be the same document, an identical document to the one sent out to the other unit. There would be the original signature of the person who signed it. All documents could be identical, only I think it was in the left bottom-hand corner there would be a list of units to whom the order was to be sent, if it was sent to several units, and in the second or third line in the top right-hand corner, the addressee would be specified. So this was in the event that it was sent by courier. However, if communications were used, then again in the lower left-hand corner would be a list of the units to whom the order should be delivered, and on the back side most frequently, most often by hand, sometimes electronically, an indication would be made as to when a particular unit received a particular document, the name of the unit and when it received it. It could be that several units would be receiving the same order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now let's turn very briefly to the unit receiving the order. What marks, if any, would the receiving unit have placed on the order if it were to be received via a courier?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: There may have been cases - I say may be - that a copy which should be archived should be accompanied by an added piece of paper on which all the units that received the order would be listed. It would be attached to the same order or on the order itself. The things changed in time, but anyway, one could see thereby that a person would sign, a person in the chain of command, whether the administrative department of the lower unit had received it or actually one of the on-duty officers that may have been there at the time, or even perhaps the commander of the unit. So the situation varied, but this service functioned in this way so that the document would reach a particular unit and that unit would have an administrative section that received the document and one of the officers would sign, saying that the order had been received, and then it would be sent back and probably archived, or the first copy of the order would be archived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Would the -- pursuant to the regulations in practice, would the unit receiving the order by courier make any notations on the actual order indicating the date and time they received the order from the higher headquarters?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't quite understand the question. Could you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's use an example. Let's say the corps command sends a written order to a brigade command headquarters via courier. Someone at the administrative section of the brigade headquarters receives the written order from the courier. So far, is that how the system would work?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes this was indeed done by the courier service between units, but sometimes the couriers would also be staff officers who would at the same time take advantage of the opportunity to tour a unit, to visit a unit, and take the orders with them. It could have been staff officers, sometimes even a high-ranking officer or someone from the operations department. Most often the person in the operations department could act as courier. Sometimes it would be an ordinary soldier, a private whose only work was to carry mail from one place to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Once the -- again using our example, once the administrative section at the brigade headquarters receives the written order from the corps headquarters via the courier, in accordance with the regulations and practice at that time, did that administrative section make any markings or indications on the order they had just received to show the date and time they had received it?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes, there was some kind of marking that the order had been received. And the order would have to be registered in one way or another in the command. But there were other situations, too. It was chaotic and disorderly. But on the whole, that is how it should have been done, and in most cases it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me turn now to documents received via the Paket system or via some other type of electronic means. When those documents were received, those orders were received, you told us they would print them out and they would -- the contents would be identical to the original order but there would be no stamp or signature on the document. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: At the receiving end, yes. But at the sending end they had the original document on the disk and the paper copy as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'm focusing now, sir, on the receiving end. Would the receiving unit that had received a written order via electronic means make any markings on that document to indicate that they had received it in accordance with the regulations and practice?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In that other unit, the regulation was that an adequate square stamp should be used with similar information as that entered at the sending end, but in this case you would fill in the column saying when the document was received. That is how it should have been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Selimovic, I'd like to turn now to a slightly different topic. You told us earlier this morning that the documents were prepared or the orders, written orders, were prepared according to a format. Can you tell the Trial Chamber briefly what that format was or what the components and characteristics of a written order were?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: If I need to describe it, then there would be a heading. In the top left-hand corner the number of the unit, the registration number of the document, when it was registered. On the right-hand side, in the corner, would be indication that it was a military secret. Then in the second line the contents of the order, briefly, what type of an order it is, and then in that line on the right to whom the order is addressed. It would be stated whether it was one unit or several units. If there was enough space, all the units would be indicated there. Then in the next line there would be a kind of introduction to the order when usually this order referred to another order from the superior command, and then after that, the order itself. There would be the word "I order," and then the main body of the document containing the substance of the order, and below that, in the left-hand corner, there could be the initials of the person who drafted, processed or typed the document. Those initials would be in the left-hand corner, and also possibly the units to whom this order was intended for. And on the right-hand side, the first and last name of the commander and his signature on the original. Or if it was sent by electronic means, then it would just state the first and last name of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Selimovic, we've -- we've talked at great length about the various procedures that were employed and the regulations that governed the use of written orders. You've also told us that the situation was a bit chaotic. Were these procedures that you've outlined for us consistently followed? In other words, did all the documents always have all of these elements?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Most of the documents did, I would say, but I can remember some documents that -- in fact, you showed me some documents earlier on from which we can see that a different procedure was applied. Some people applied the knowledge they had acquired earlier on or the instructions they were given, but some individuals would adapt things, so the document may appear differently and some of those elements may have been left out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You've told us that some people may have applied knowledge they had acquired earlier. Are there any other reasons why there might be slight variations between different orders coming from the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid the question is not quite clear to me. I'm sorry. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me try to rephrase the question for you. You've told us that there might have been slight variations among the documents or that items may have been missing that you would expect to see on the documents. One of the reasons you've told us was because people may have used knowledge that they'd acquired earlier. Can you tell us any other reasons why the systems and procedures and regulations might not have always been 100 per cent complied with in the 3rd Corps during 1993.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: In most cases it depended on the personnel. There were professionals who knew what an order should look like, and there were others who encountered such things for the first time, it was their first time for them to write an order, and that is why there may have been differences. I can't remember any other special example, but sometimes there may have been problems because the communications system was not perhaps working too well and a message had to be repeated. Then only a part of the document would go through and then it had to be sent again. But things like that could happen. But I think what I first said is the main reason for the variations, because the electronic system did provide for the document being identical -- the content of the document to be identical once it is sent through electronic media.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What impact, if any, did the tempo of combat operations have on following procedures with respect to written orders?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: In any event, the tempo did have some effect. Orders may have been done in haste. Sometimes it would be one person who would complete the order himself. This also may have been a reason that some documents were abbreviated with some items or parts left out, but it had to convey the gist of the order, what the order was telling the person at the other end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Selimovic, based on the time that you served as the chief of communications for the 3rd Corps in 1993, were you aware of any instances where unauthorised orders were transmitted from the 3rd Corps headquarters; that is, orders that the commander disagreed with or did not approve?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't recollect any such particular situation, but I have said that there were people who would appear, and we down there would realise that they had been sent by someone, and they started signing. I can be specific and give you a particular instance of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me just ask you before -- I will ask you to elaborate on that, but is this the only instance that you recall any such instance?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: I said that occasionally the people from the operations section would sign a document. In my view, perhaps they shouldn't have, but I think that it did happen occasionally. But this would apply more to reports. The operations officer on duty might sign a document, but not orders, mostly reports. Sometimes individuals would get things mixed up and they might sign an order as well. Now, whether the commander sanctioned this, I don't know. I can't remember. He may have orally let them know that this is something they shouldn't do, but I don't -- I can't be any more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So you certainly don't recall any specific instances where that happened other than the one incident?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know of that one instance. I don't know whether it is really linked to that particular question, but I think that such a situation did arise. General Mahmuljin appeared in the corps command, and suddenly he started signing some orders, and the corps commander was in the field at the forward command post. The chief of staff, I think, was in an operations group or something like that. I don't know where the deputy was. But anyway, I did see such a signature by this person, and I actually didn't know who he was. Later on, I heard about him, that he had become a commander and that he had come from the General Staff, the Supreme Command. But just at that moment, I didn't know who he was. And the soldiers who were meant to send them, these orders on, they were confused, wondering what it was. But later on this was settled. But for a time there was this unknown person who was signing on behalf of the commander. On the electronic copy, there would be just the printed name "Enver Hadzihasanovic," and on the original Mahmuljin would be -- Mahmuljin's signature would appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate date or month and year in which this happened?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was halfway through 1993. Perhaps in June. I can't be sure. Or perhaps it was in the second half or 1993, but that was, roughly speaking, the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're at the point in time where I would ask the witness be shown original orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And for the benefit of the witness, sir, what I'm going to do is show you four documents, one at a time. To your left is a machine that will allow us all to watch exactly what document it is that you're looking at, and I'm going to ask you to indicate on the document some of these various components and characteristics that you have already told us about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the first such document is contested document 162. And again for the record, copies of these documents have been previously provided. I would ask that this now be shown to the witness, and after the witness has had a chance to look at it, if he could please put it onto the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, Witness, I will not be asking you any questions about the contents of the document, simply on the form and format and markings on the document. Sir, have you had an opportunity to look at this document?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please -- and I'd ask that the witness be provided with some kind of pointer or something that he can -- Sir, if you could -- let's start at the top of the document. There are two places where there are numbers that are circled at the top of the document. Do you have any idea what those circled numbers represent? And if you -- if you -- sorry, if you do speak of -- of any of the markings, if you could please point to it so we all know exactly what it is you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: You're referring to these two numbers at the top. These numbers were subsequently added. That is obvious. I don't know, perhaps it indicates the time. I really don't know. It's very odd. Perhaps it -- it's the time when someone processed the document or received it. It's not customary for someone in the communications centre to add such numbers. Someone who had this document in his hands at a later date must have done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please now proceed, starting with the written or typewritten script on the upper left and just, again, tell us what these elements are on the document.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: So this document obviously comes from the 3rd Corps Command. This is more or less how we would register the document. The first two numbers usually refer to the function of the document. This document had this number, which allowed one to recognise the document to be one from a certain department or from a certain person. And then we have the date indicating when the document was drafted, typed out. As I said, in the right-hand corner it mentions the degree of confidentiality. I haven't said this yet, but it says "Urgent" here, and that means that when the document is received in the communications centre, it has to be forwarded as soon as possible to the command to which it is addressed. This part under "Order," it doesn't say what the contents are, it just says who it is to be forwarded to, and this is the initial part that has to do with the assessment or the evaluation of the situation.
