I mentioned the part under "Order," and there are a number of items which state what the orders are. In the right-hand corner, it says "Commander, Enver Hadzihasanovic," and it says "Signed and stamped -- verified with signature and stamp." But as far as I remember, this isn't General Hadzihasanovic's signature, with which I'm more or less familiar, so someone else must have signed it, because this is not a signature that I'm familiar with. So this is an assumption I'm making, that perhaps Muradif Mekic signed the document, although I can't be certain [Realtime transcript read in error "concern"]. If I may turn the document over. This is the rectangular stamp that I have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: And you can see that it was received by the 3rd Corps communications centre, and it was entered into an internal register of theirs. And "Handed over" has been underlined, and then we have the date and the year and the time, and it mentions the persons who sent the document or, rather, who drafted the document. I think this is some sort of indication too, some sort of electronic reference for the document which was probably made in the communications centre, by some official in the communications centre. This is a number that was obviously added later on. Perhaps it's an archives number or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, let me -- let me ask you a couple of follow-on questions, and you will see those eight-digit numbers --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague said that on page 46, line 3 -- page 46, line 3, according to the transcript, it says the witness who was speaking about whose signature it might be on the document, he said "I assume it was Muradif Mekic who signed the document," and then it says something, but he said I'm not sure, I can't be certain, but "concern" and "certain" is not the same thing. So perhaps my colleague could ask this question again or perhaps the witness could confirm what he said with regard to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I thank my colleague from the Defence with respect to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, there appears to be an error in the English transcript. Can you please turn this document back over, and again if you could look, please, at the -- not the typed signature block but the actual handwritten signature, and tell us about that if you know anything about that signature.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know whose signature this is. I can make an assumption, but I really never came across this signature. I know what General Hadzihasanovic's signature looks like, because later on I was in the Joint Command, and I would see this signature. I would see the signature of General Dzemal Merdan. I have a document that he signed, too. But this is a signature I really am not familiar with, but I can make certain assumptions. I can assume that it might be Muradif Mekic's signature. I don't know what else to say because I'm not certain. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. If you could now turn the document over, I have a few follow-on questions concerning the stamp at the top of the document. You told us that the first line indicates the time the document was received at the communications centre. Is that what you've told us?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. In the first line you have the number of an internal register in the communications centre. There was some sort of register, and this document was recorded under a certain number. An official in the communications centre did that. The number I'm referring to is 1768.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the next line indicates precisely what?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: It indicates that the document was handed over. It was sent. It says "Handed over." That means sent. The word "Handed over" has been underlined. That means it was handed over. From the other page, on the second page, in the other command -- on the other side there was an identical document and it must have been received since the stamp is a universal one. So on the other side they would have underlined the word "Received," but this is a document from the 3rd Corps, which means that it was handed over from the 3rd Corps. And on the -- in the other line we have the date, the year, the date, and the time when the document was handed over, that is to say when it was forwarded by electronic means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So just so that I'm clear, sir, you're telling us that this stamp -- or from this stamp we know that this document was sent on the 17th of April, 1993, at 2245 hours?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So the word that's underlined meaning "Handed over," in fact means it was sent?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the signature at the bottom, do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: It's probably one of the officials from the communications centre. I'll try to read it. Ademovic. Ademovic, if I'm reading it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That signature would --

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think that there was an official who had that name in the communications centre. I think I can remember him. That's his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What does that signature --

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: That was a person in the communications centre. This means that the document was received and sent in the communications centre and that this person will claim that the document was sent to the forwarding address. That was that person's responsibility. He had certain responsibilities, certain duties he had to perform in the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Selimovic, immediately above that signature there are a number of what appear to be abbreviations. Can you tell us what those abbreviations stand for?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think that these abbreviations were noted down in the communications centre, too, and that this is in fact the electronic title of the document. I don't know if you understand what I'm saying. The name of the file, the abbreviated name of the file. It would be the abbreviated name of the electronic file.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. With the assistance of the usher, I would ask that that document be retrieved and the next document, which is CD, or contested document, 35 be provided to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, sir, I'll be asking you the same types of questions. If you could just take a moment to look at that document. And again I will not be asking you questions concerning the substance of the document. Okay. Again, sir, if you could point out some of the characteristics of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: At the top, again I can't say what it is. Perhaps it indicates the time or it's some sort of internal number for a register in the administration. Perhaps it was a number that was given to the document when it was being processed, but I really don't know. Perhaps it's some sort of internal number for the document. Again this is quite usual. This is what documents usually looked like. You have the name of the unit, the name of the document, the number of the document, the time. It says "Military secret." And then it says "Query," and "Forward to." It says who the document should be forwarded to. There's an introduction, and then we have the main contents. These are the initials of someone who prepared the document and typed it out. So this refers to the person who drafted the document and to the person who typed it out. On the right-hand side, it says "Commander, Enver Hadzihasanovic," and we have a different signature here, and there is the word "za," which means "for," as I said. So a pen was used to add the word "za" meaning "for," and we have the signature and the circular stamp of the 3rd Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, before we turn the document over, do you recognise the signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a little confused. I can't recognise the signature right now, but it's not General Hadzihasanovic's signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. If you could please turn the document over. Again there's a number of handwritten markings on the very top line of the document.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Again we have this -- well, let's say electronic number or name of the file. This is the number they used in the communications centre, and this was probably the time when the document was sent. We have this rectangular stamp again, and it says that the number in the communication centre register under which it was registered is 2426. This means that the document was sent, so the word "Sent" has been underlined. It was sent via communications centre on the 12th of July, 1993, at 1408 hours. It says that it was processed or, rather, drafted by - I can't read the signature right now - Music, Mesic. And here it's -- it states the type of radio communications that was used. The circled letters here mean that the document was sent by Paket communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just so that we're clear then, sir, the line or series of abbreviations on the line where there is a circle immediately above the signature is a place where the communications centre could indicate the method by which the document was sent. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, what those abbreviations stand for, beginning with the one on the far left, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Some documents of the former JNA were used. So all possible types of communications were listed, all the various forms of communications that people were familiar with at the time. "TLP" means teleprinter. "TGR" means a telegram or the Morse code. "TLF" means phone. "RRV" means radio relay communication. "ZV," I think that means wire communication. And finally there is "RV." It's not very clear. It should say "RV." That means radio communication. And this means that it was sent by Paket communications. That's the type of communications concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again with the assistance of the usher, I would ask that that document be returned to the Prosecution table and that the witness be shown contested document 41.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, at the top, as I have already said, it's probably some kind of internal number that was used by someone in the administrative department or in the archives. Perhaps this is a number used in the archives, since it's in red. I have the impression that this is some sort of a number that was used in the archives, an internal number of some sort. Again, this is quite common. You can see that the document comes from the 3rd Corps, and here it says "Military secret." I really don't know what this number is. Here it says "Order," "Forward to," and it says who the document should be forwarded to. We have an introduction. It says: "I hereby order..." And then we have the contents of the order. Here we have the initials of someone who drafted the document and typed it out. In the lower right-hand corner, it says "Commander, Enver Hadzihasanovic," certified, verified with a stamp. I can recognise this signature. It is Dzemal Merdan's signature, if I remember this correctly. I think it is Dzemal Merdan. And again we have the word "For" here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, if you could turn that document over. Again, if you're able to tell us what the markings on the back of this document are, please.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Again we have the electronic name for the file, the computer file. I've already mentioned this, the number used in the communications centre. Again we have the stamp from communications centre. This is the internal number used by an official in the communications centre. The number is 1711. We have the word "Sent," which has been underlined. This means that the document was sent from the 3rd Corps Command, from the communications centre, and the date is the 6th of September, 1993. It was sent at 1710 hours. You can't see how the document was sent. If someone had done this properly, he would have indicated the means used to send the document. And here we have the signature of the person who sent the document to a certain unit. The name is Alic, if I can read it correctly. This would be an official in the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With again the assistance of the usher, I would ask that the witness be shown one last document. This is contested document 649. For the record, document CD41 has been returned to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Witness, if you could please tell us any distinguishing features of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Once again, we can see the document was drafted in the 3rd Corps Command, the number of the document, the time it was issued, an indication that it is a military secret, the degree of secrecy. Then a brief summary of the contents, indicating the type of document it is, to whom it is addressed, and then, underlined, the unit it is addressed to. Now, here we have an additional stamp. This is the 325th Mountain Brigade. It is their verification that the document reached their command, and the number under which it was registered and the time when it arrived at the command. So clearly this document went by courier. Then the introduction, then the order, and then the main points of the order. Attached to this document we see that there's an annex. This is probably what follows the order. Then there's an indication that it is the commander, Enver Hadzihasanovic, without a signature. However, as this document is linked together, we see that the plan was approved by the chief of staff, Muradif Mekic. And his signature, probably his signature. As I was saying, I don't say that I'm a hundred per cent sure, but as chief of staff, he approved such a plan. Now, why there's no signature by the commander, obviously he didn't see it. It must have been seen by the chief of staff, that somehow he either prepared it or took part in its preparation or ordered it to be prepared. So then comes the plan itself, and that is the plan of the visit to units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, could you please look on the back of this document, computer printout document. Do you see any markings on the back of the document?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you explain why this document has no markings unlike the previous three documents we looked at?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: This document did not go to the communications centre. I can see that it was not sent through the communications centre. It probably went by courier. That is the most probable explanation. As far as I can see, it was signed by Mekic Muradif, followed by his signature, probably his signature. Now, whether the commander saw this or not, I really don't know, but there's no signature of his there. Now, whether the document may have been in the computer, but in anyway, I can see from this that it was received by the 325th Mountain Brigade. And here there's an indication that it was sent to the Municipal Staff of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask that that document be returned to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Selimovic, I thank you very much for your answers and your willingness again to meet with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I also would like to thank my friends from the Defence for allowing me to lead the evidence of this witness today. The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I now give the floor to the Defence counsel for their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We will cross-examine the witness but only with respect to the questions that he has discussed with the Prosecutor. So we, too, will only limit our questions to the questions indicated by the Trial Chamber in their oral order.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Selimovic. Though we know one another, for the record let me introduce myself. I'm Edina Residovic, and I am representing General Enver Hadzihasanovic. You've already told my learned friend that in the Yugoslav People's Army you were an officer with a rank of captain first class and that throughout your service in the JNA you were involved with communications; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, answering those questions you confirmed that throughout your professional career, first in the Yugoslav People's Army and then in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and finally in the Federation army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, you were always linked to the communications system; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As chief of communications, you joined the 3rd Corps in November 1993 when that corps or the command of that corps was actually established; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have already said that you were an organ for planning and organising communications, but is it also true that there was a communications company in the command which directly dealt with the reception and dispatch of certain documents, orders, and other documents through the established communications system? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, the communications system was housed in the basement of the 3rd Corps headquarters, which before the war had been used by the Zenica steelworks as a nuclear shelter, that is a shelter which administrative buildings had to provide in accordance with the law that was in force at the time.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can remember, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have already explained that at first your working conditions were very difficult. My question is: Is it true that as a professional officer specialising in communications, you managed quite quickly to draw up a plan of possible communications in the 3rd Corps but it took several months and maybe, for some communications, even a whole year before those plans were implemented? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You explained the conditions under which you were working, but in order to ask you a few more specific questions, I shall repeat some of the difficulties you encountered. First of all, you were short of certain communications devices, and what little you had were frequently outdated, and you didn't have the possibilities to repair them. Most of the high-quality communications equipment was taken by the Yugoslav People's Army, and there were many other obstacles to the system you were establishing working on a regular basis and efficiently.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The situation really was a difficult one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that you had radio equipment. Is it true that these were radios which you received mainly by using the old radio equipment of the Territorial Defence, whereas others were mobilised or requisitioned from radio amateurs?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My learned friend asked you about telephone communications and the use of the PTT system of communications. My question is: Am I right in saying that in the course of 1993, this system was still highly unreliable and that, due to various circumstances and particularly the war, was frequently down so that it was not a communications system you could rely on. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Answering one of the questions from my learned friend, you said that there was jamming and sometimes a message had to be sent repeatedly or it simply couldn't reach its destination. So my question is: Am I right in saying that at the beginning of 1993, when overt conflicts broke out between the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HVO, a powerful jamming device was left in the hands of the HVO so that throughout 1993 you had a lot of problems with interception and jamming or breakdown of your communications. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, as you have already explained, investing a maximum of effort and all your skill and knowledge, you did gradually manage to set up a -- quite a reliable communications system. Tell me, is it true that this establishment was done as follows: First of all, you yourself, in addition to the radios, came into the possession of modems and computers, and then you managed to link them up in such a way that they could be used as communications devices through which encrypted packets could be sent, and up until March 1993 was your Paket connection with the Supreme Command, was that the process through which you started establishing the communications system?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think that at the beginning of that year, we did have a Paket, one channel of communications with somebody in the General Staff. In those days I didn't know who it was we had communication with, but somebody in the General Staff. This was at the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was only later, after the establishment of this Paket system with the General Staff or the Supreme Command, you gradually procured modems and radio devices which you supplied certain brigades with, and only once those brigades had the same devices as you yourself were you able to communicate with them through these Paket communications; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Quantities were limited and few, so that it was really difficult to find a computer and a modem and link it all up with an operator who would be able to use them, and only then could it be set in motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Though you said that earlier on, in addition to devices you were also short of qualified personnel, so that parallel with the establishment of the system, you planned training of personnel and provided basic training so that you did your best to train operators to use those devices. However, in spite of all these efforts, it could be said that a complete system was not established with all the units and brigades within the 3rd Corps by the end of 1993. Is that true, or did you already have Paket communications with all brigades in the course of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: We did have them mostly by the end of 1993 with all the brigades. However, again there was the question of security or reliability. This was a daily problem: You establish a system but the next day it breaks down, a device is destroyed, or a computer. But a system as a system did exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Once you established this system, you have already said that one of the problems was the breakdown of the system, but you also said that once it was established, you could only send brief messages using that system, of one to two pages.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: People who have any knowledge about these matters, because of the speed of transmission, the quantity was limited. Every document of any weight - that is how we referred to it - meaning the quantity of information contained or, rather, the number of pages that the document consisted of could not be sent in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be right to say, Mr. Selimovic, that while the system was operational, when both sides had the devices and the operators and there was no jamming or breakdowns, that a certain report going from the 3rd Corps could be sent to a certain unit or brigade in only a few minutes, but due to the problems that we have just referred to, sometimes it took several hours and sometimes even several days before it could be sent. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, throughout 1993, you were unable to establish a communications system that would be reliable with units that were resubordinated to the brigades, that is battalions, companies, and platoons. Their system mainly relied on couriers or radios, depending on the configuration of the ground and other circumstances that affected this.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: The lower down we went, it was more and more difficult to maintain communications. In fact, we were constrained by the number of devices, which we were short of.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will now ask you about a particular situation. Within a normal system of communications, a lower-level unit sends reports and information to a superior command and then that command to the command above it in the hierarchy. Is it true to say that sometimes communications would break down completely between, for instance, a brigade and an operations group, and then the brigade would use the communications centre of the 3rd Corps as a means of sending information to a superior command? Do you remember any such situations when the 3rd Corps communications centre was used to bridge a breakdown between a brigade and a superior command?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were such situations. Sometimes the brigade command was close to the operations group command, and then a report would be sent to that address and not to the proper address. It -- it didn't end up in the communications centre of that particular unit but, rather, in a lower-level unit and then the report would go to the higher-level unit, or vice versa. There were such situations in this general confusion and chaos and combat operations, and the absence of communications devices required that we somehow get round it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to several questions from my learned friend, you indicated how you monitored how a document or order went from the 3rd Corps to a subordinated unit. This was usually done, in the documents that we have seen, by documents reaching operations groups, brigades, or Municipal Staffs. Tell me, please, is it true that you were not able to follow what happened with that order after that, because you in the communications system in the 3rd Corps had no way of monitoring to see whether that order went beyond the brigade or, rather, whether the battalion, platoon, or the foot soldier had been informed of it.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the principle. A superior goes to the first subordinate, and then it goes from there downwards according to the chain of command. So that I didn't have any knowledge as to how the document moved down the chain.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to a question from my colleagues, you spoke in detail about your own knowledge based on your experience from the former JNA and your professional training with respect to the drafting of orders and other corps documents, and you illustrated this with a number of examples. I should now like to ask you: Is it true that there was a certain difference between basic orders, combat orders - which may be an order for an attack or for defence - and certain specialised orders? Let me explain what I mean. Is it true that what you -- the explanations you gave regarding teamwork, that applied more to a group of specialists in the staff working together on combat orders with complicated assignments to units, whereas certain specialist orders could have been compiled by individual officers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As I'm quite sure my learned friend has far more knowledge of the military than myself, I won't go into those military orders in further detail, but I felt it was important. There were certain types of orders which by nature of things were more complicated than others which were led simply to a particular area. For example, the organisation of communications in a particular unit, you might have sent a message to somebody in the unit there to say receive this device or set up a communications system, something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The technical aspect for the functioning of a particular system, if something needed to be added or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also explaining the way in which documents were sent through the communications centre, you showed us that the person, according to the internal organisation, was - at that point in time operating the communications device - was duty-bound to fill in a certain stamp indicating when the document was sent, and he would sign to confirm that that information is correct.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also explained that the person at the other end in the receiving unit, receiving the order, had a similar stamp when -- on which that person would sign that he had received the document.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, is it true that that unit was not under any obligation to send back that document, with the stamp that it had been received, to the 3rd Corps Command?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you would be quite certain that the order had been received only if you were able to check with the unit you sent it to that the order had indeed been received. Otherwise, you in the communications system would not know whether the message that was sent was intercepted, interrupted, or in fact received.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also answered the question as to who the persons were who signed certain orders. You said it was the commander, the deputy commander, and the chief of staff. Tell me, please, were there any instances of a person being given special authorisation by the commander to sign a particular document, and for persons sending the document to the communications centre, that would be enough to show that that person could sign?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: If the people in the administration section put a stamp on it, then it could have been sent from the communications centre with a different signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me then ask you: Is it true that in the communications centre you would receive or accept every document that had a signature and a stamp because you felt that the first check had been done by someone else? The communications centre was not the entity controlling or checking whether the signature was of an authorised person or not.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So this administrative or protocol service, or whatever it was called, was the service whose duty it was to check whether the document was signed by an authorised person or not; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We've seen several documents which says "Commander, Enver Hadzihasanovic," but signed by others. Some signatures you have recognised, others you're not sure about. Actually, in the communications centre, when you receive a document, for you it is a document that has to be sent; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, at the moment you're sending the document, you don't know whether the commander has seen that document or not at all?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Lower-ranking people cannot make any such verifications. For them, it's valid document if it is signed and if it bears a stamp. The stamp was maybe even more important. It was even more decisive than the actual signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Though it is now time for the break, I have only one or two questions left. Perhaps I could finish off before the break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's better to have the break, because it is already half past twelve, and we will resume at five to 1.00, and the Judges will have some questions after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give the floor to the Defence now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When answering a question put to you by my learned colleague from the Prosecution, you said that at the beginning you would receive a signed and certified document in the communications centre, and you would then type it out and forward it through electronic means. Is that true -- would it be true to say that that happened at the beginning of 1993, until the first computers arrived in the corps, computers on which one could type?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, as you explained, when the 3rd Corps received the computers, from that time onwards you would receive a disk with the original document, a disk on which the text of the document would be contained, and you would forward that text from the disk to the units to which the document had been addressed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you explained, it wasn't possible to send signatures and stamps through electronic means, so that the unit receiving the document didn't know who actually had signed the document, whether it had been the commander whose name was printed out or some other person on behalf of the commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you were given computers in order to facilitate the work for all professional officers who were drafting these orders, would it be correct to say that the computers contained certain types of orders or documents? There was, for example, a copy of an order, and there was a heading in the computer indicating that the 3rd Corps Command was concerned, and there would be the signature of the commander. The official who processed the document would add other information and the contents of the order, whereas the block signature and the heading were in the computer on a permanent basis and would be used in each order. Are you aware of the fact that there was a record of the block signature in the computer at all times?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, on the whole that is how it was. Quite frequently we used a previous file to compile the next file if the contents were identical. We always tried to do what was most efficient and most rapid.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you explained to us in detail that it was the duty of the administrative staff to check whether the person who had signed the document was an authorised person, you don't know, and in fact you don't have any information whether it was possible for you to receive a document from someone who had no authority at all, and you don't know how this was possible.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I wasn't even in a position to check this, because in the communications centre, if there was a signature and a stamp, it was a legitimate document. As to checking these things, as a rule we didn't do this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a chief -- as the chief of the communications centre and when communicating with your communications company, could you confirm that one couldn't rule out the possibility of such signatures being abused?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, in principle.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't mean causing any damage of any kind, but I'm referring to documents containing the name of a commander that was signed by people who were supposed to sign such documents.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was something that could happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, you cited a number of examples. For example, examples of people who had signed documents although they had no authorisation to do so. I have one more question. You described to us in detail the circulation of documents from the time a document was drafted. You described the preparation of the document and how documents were forwarded to certain units. My question is: Would it be correct to say that in the communications centre in the 3rd Corps you weren't able to follow the circulation of documents in units that were subordinated to you? I'll be a little clearer. You weren't able to follow orders of the brigade commanders or battalion commanders. So you weren't able to follow how these orders were forwarded to the subordinate units, and you weren't able to control information that the leaders of companies would send to other units. Is it true that you never had contact with such documents?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I have some questions that follow on from the questions that have just been put to you. In response to a question from the Prosecution, you said that you were in charge of forwarding documents as part of your responsibilities. Did you just have to deal with the issue of orders forwarded to external units, or did you have other responsibilities? For example, the issue of radio frequencies, the logistical equipment provided to units involved in communications? Wasn't your role more important than that of a person who was just responsible for forwarding orders? Could you answer that question, please.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: I was describing the communications system and described my own role. I carried out those duties, but you are quite correct, I carried out those staff duties, too, and I also had to manage the frequencies used. That is something that has to be done when dealing with the communications plan. You have to establish the sort of frequencies and devices that will be used. So perhaps I haven't presented you with a very accurate picture in that I didn't directly draft messages and send messages. A unit in the 3rd Corps that had been designated for this was responsible for such matters, but I knew more about the communications system as a professional, and I tried to develop the most efficient communications system possible because it was difficult to operate such a system and establish such a system. So in the staff, I was the one who knew the most about such communication systems. So I was closest to the soldiers in the communications units who were involved in forwarding orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your premises were in -- located in the headquarters. How many officers or soldiers did you have under you, and how many rooms did you have for your mission?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: This number changed. On the whole, the department had up to about three employees, and I was the chief. That was in the communications department, and it was part of the 3rd Corps staff. And there was also a communications company that dealt with forwarding and receiving messages within the communications system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this company, this communications company, you were in charge of them, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the name of the person who was in charge of the company responsible for forwarding messages?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, according to the hierarchy of the 3rd Corps Command, since I wasn't in a position to command, I didn't have such duties. I couldn't even make use of that unit. I knew what it was supposed to do, but they were linked to the chief of staff of the 3rd Corps. And that is the case today, more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the orders that you were shown a minute ago, but I'll go back to that, how many people did you have at your disposal who, after they received disks, used a modem or a radio system to send orders to the outside? How many people were under you who were involved in such work?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: In that department, there was an organ for cryptographic protection very often, and they were closer to that system of sending messages, because they should have known how a cryptographic system was used. They were familiar with the rules for cryptographic protection so they would be closer to that unit that was involved in receiving documents, encrypting them and sending them to other units. So that's what this unit in the communications company did. And sometimes with my associates I had the possibility of controlling how they worked or the possibility of helping them if there was anything I could help them with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that the orders that you saw, thanks to the computers that your department had been provided with, would arrive on a disk and then the disk would be used to relay the orders to the outside. The computers that the 3rd Corps had, do you know what brand of computers they had?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know some of them. At the time, I think they had IBMs perhaps. A 286, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So roughly speaking, how many computers did the 3rd Corps have? Could you give us a rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, we started working with only one computer. We had a very limited number of computers, just a couple at the beginning of 1993. I don't believe that we had more than three or four computers of different kinds at the time. They'd been commandeered from certain organisations where such computers could be found at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So they were IBM computers that had been commandeered from certain companies. What happened to these computers and the disks? Do you know what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as technology developed and time passed, we received, I'd say, other computers, 386 computers, for example. Sometimes such a new computer would appear and that's how this processed developed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the old computers, what happened to them? Were they thrown in the trash? Were they handed over to certain departments in Bosnia? What happened to these computers? As far as you know. If you don't know, just say so.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, these computers were used as much as that was possible. They were fully exploited, and I think, if I may say so, that some of them remained in warehouses. Many of them have remained there to this very day, and many of them were destroyed, damaged in the fighting. Some of them were seized. Various things happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If we follow the circulation or the process of drafting an order as far as we have understood this, because it's not very clear for me yet, it's not totally clear for me, an order is drafted by, let's say, the 3rd Corps Commander, either by himself or by someone who works under him. This order is drafted and then with a -- it's drafted with the help of the computer the 3rd Corps has. There is a disk taken from this computer, and the floppy disk is used to edit the document on the outside. Can you confirm that that is the process followed?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the computer has a floppy disk. You insert it, you record the document on the hard disk, and then you send it on, and the floppy disk is then returned to the person who sent it to the communications centre, together with the original document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Between the communications centre and the 3rd Corps Command office, are all the computers linked up or was it necessary to take a floppy disk from the office of the commander of the 3rd Corps, take it to the communications centre in order to have it forwarded or was there a network that was in existence?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: At the time the corps commander didn't have a computer. We just had a computer in the communications centre. Perhaps at the very beginning. That was in the office that was near the administrative department, and there was an official who helped to find the relevant document on the computer. We didn't have a network of any kind. We didn't have such possibilities. We didn't even know what a network was at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm still not quite clear. The single computer that you seem to have had at the beginning, where was it located?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: In the 3rd Corps communications centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I have understood you correctly, the secretary of the 3rd Corps commander would use a typewriter to type out a text. This text would then be taken to the computer in the communications centre and that's when the text would be downloaded on a disk and then a modem was used and it would be relayed to the outside. Is that correct? Is that the process followed? You're nodding. Please say it out aloud.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, but that's the first stage. At the time there were no other computers in the command that would allow one to advance the process of drafting documents. As soon as we received the second computer, it was put into operation. And there was an additional one, there was a third one. But initially we just had one computer in the communications centre, and we didn't need a floppy disk at the time. We'd type out the text directly onto the hard disk because the computer was, at the time, a means of communications and - how should I put it? - it was used both for administrative needs and for communications purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like you to be shown the documents that you've already been shown. Document 649. Put it on the ELMO. You have document 649 before you. At the top and to the left you can see the date, the 11th of March, 1993. Above we have the number 02/742. The three other documents that you were shown had the numbers 02/33. Isn't the number 33 missing in this document? Because the three other documents - we can show them to you - have the number 02/33, and then there is another number. 02 should correspond to the command of the 3rd Corps. Number 33, what does that correspond to? We'll show you document number 41. Could you place document 41 on the ELMO. As you can see, this document, we still have the number 02, but we have number 33 as well, and this is a number that doesn't appear in the first document you were shown. In your opinion, what does this number represent, number 33?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'm really not a specialist. I didn't deal with this task. A different service dealt with it. They would then have to have this matter defined. As far as I can remember, the first two numbers, for example 02, I think that's the number designating the corps. I think this was done in the corps. These are things that changed, you know. This changed as someone read through something or knew something. But number 33 might have to do with some sort of a function or type of document since there were orders and reports and -- well, let's say warnings as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you can't answer that question. You can see that there are numbers 542, 2236. All the numbers -- all the documents have numbers. If we follow the chronological order from the 1st of January, 1993, that must be number 1 on the hard disk of the computer, it should be possible to find, if this was typed on the computer, the totality of the documents, all these documents.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it should be possible to find them on the computer. It should be possible to find all the documents there. Either in the archives or on the computer, although this can be deleted from the computer from time to time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In fact, you can delete this, but you can't erase anything from a hard disk. We'll show you document 162 now. Could you have a look at the stamp on page 2 of this document. In the penultimate line, you -- you mentioned what TLF, telex, et cetera, means. How is it that in this document we don't know the means used to forward the document? None of these letters have been encircled. None of these indications have been encircled. How could you explain this? As you can see --

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: As a rule, the person who signed this should have encircled the means of communications used. Obviously the person failed to do that. He didn't correctly do what he should have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The person who processed the document, Ademovic who signed it, how would he have the document sent; by telephone, by telex, by radio, by amateur radio system? What would he do given that there's no indication as to how this document should be sent?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: There was an unwritten rule according to which a document should be sent to the point it was supposed to arrive at by using the most efficient and the most rapid means. So you would use the best communications line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you can see it says 2245 hours. So there was certainly no postman or courier at the time. So how would this order be sent? Would a telephone be used, a telex? What would happen in such a situation? Because it was sent at 2245 hours, but we don't know how.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the person processing this document obviously didn't complete his work and didn't indicate the means of communication used to send the document. I assume that Paket communications or a telephone modem was used to send the document. I think Paket communications were used. It was sent to the Krajina operations group by Paket communications. It must have been sent by Paket communications. That's what should be indicated on the end, a radio link. It's not very legible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the order was sent at 2245 hours, one might think that the order was drafted half an hour or five minutes earlier. When one sends a document at such a late time, it means that it's urgent, or is that not the case? And my question -- well, the answer is contained in the document, because I can see that there is the word "Urgent" that appears on the first page. If you have a look at the first page, you will see it. So you were a superior officer. In your opinion, was such an order drafted immediately prior to 2245 hours, given the urgent nature of the document?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the document was drafted perhaps an hour or two before it was sent, but there is a certain procedure of circulation. The document has to be signed, certified. The courier has to take it to the communications centre. This takes a certain time. And then sometimes the document would be kept by the person who drafted it for a certain amount of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But isn't it the person who drafted it and signed it who should determine how the order should be forwarded? Isn't it for the person who has drafted the order - isn't this usually the case in the army - isn't it for this person to say whether it should be sent by telephone, telex, by courier? And if that is the case, why is nothing stated about this on page 1?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: As I have already said, we were developing this system to the extent that we had knowledge about it. We tried to ensure that it functioned, but it's obvious that not everything was done. So here we have no indication as to how the document should be sent, that's true, but all fairly short documents could often be processed by the communications centre. They could be sent by the communications centre. But for lengthy documents it was difficult for the communications centre to send them, so the person who drafted the document or if a person was aware of the importance of a document or that someone might find out about the document, in such cases a courier was used to deliver the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You had the impression, because the Defence asked you about this, and you answered by saying that there was indeed jamming, and you said that one might be tapped. So do you believe that orders which were not encrypted may come to be known by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: The soldiers who were working in the communications centre knew that they must not, on an open line, send orders or documents. So that by developing this system for encryption and communication, we used that system. And in that case, some documents which were a military secret could be sent through the communications system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Using the Paket system and what was sent by telex, did the army have its own network or did you have to use the PTT network, which is the normal network? Were you dependent upon the civilian network or did you have your own network?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: We used parts of the telecom or PTT system. For instance, I already said that as far as Kakanj, we did have a line, a wire line, so that then the document would be sent by telephone modems. But, for instance, in the direction of Bosanska Krajina throughout the period almost, we didn't have any wire connections, but the only communications possible was by Paket. So written information could be sent in that form only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you correctly, you were the person responsible for the entire communications system of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was the most responsible system [as interpreted] for the functioning of the communications system.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Most responsible person. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did this communications system function round the clock? Was there a duty officer at the level of the communications centre?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: The communications company had certain communications centre functioning all the time. That would be at the basic command post and at the forward command post. We planned work on around-the-clock basis, and people took shifts. The staff members worked in shifts, but there was duty work all the time. Sometimes the shift would be 12 hours or 24 hours, depending on the circumstances. And that was the customary method of work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The duty officer in the communications, he had a register in which he noted down everything that happened, that he received a telex, a phone call. Did he have a register in which he noted down all those things? If a unit in a field would call up at 2.00 a.m., saying that there was fire being opened at them, would this officer note all that down?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the communications centre there would be an officer in charge, usually a non-commissioned officer by rank, whose duty it was to make sure that the communications centre should function as best it could at that point in time. He was of a slightly higher rank than the regular operator, and this communications centre was an element of the operations centre, and the operations centre there was an officer who would at times enter the communications centre and might receive a message either there or in the operations centre, or he would get a written document received by the communications centre just then and handed over to him at such a late hour. And then he would decide whether to wake the commander or not if the commander should be asleep, if he was asleep at such a late hour, or perhaps he himself would deal with the situation because the operations centre functioned parallel with the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Judges have no other questions for the witness. Does the Defence have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In answer to a question from the Presiding Judge in connection to the writing of documents, it is still a bit unclear to me, so I would like to ask you to clarify. Is my understanding of the situation correct; namely, when you were describing how an order or some other document was compiled, you spoke about the preparations for that order, and am I right in understanding that most of the orders, as a draft, would be prepared and typed by one of the staff officers, to be shown to the commander?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, most frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So very rarely would the commander himself dictate an order to his secretary. He would mostly receive a draft order that you may have drafted in response to his idea or on your own initiative and then he would sign the document?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: In most cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My next question has to do with these numbers. Probably in the corps command there must have been some record of what each number meant, and if we were to find those records, we would know what 01, 02, et cetera, all the other numbers, mean?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My next question is linked to what you have just explained. The communications system worked round-the-clock as well as the operations centre of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were crews, there were staff working in that centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But earlier on you explained that there were frequent interruptions on the lines, and as people were working non-stop, when there were interruptions it would be quite possible that they would send a document in the night that they may have received a day before but were unable to send it before the connection was re-established.

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And is it true to say that in wartime, at night it is easier to establish a connection than during the day?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Not necessarily so. It's not really linked to the time of day or night.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question linked to communications. You have explained the various devices, but as the communications centre was working all night so that couriers in that communications company were also available 24 hours, and whenever necessary, they could carry a message if something was urgent?

utterances.speaker: SENAD SELIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, if it could not be sent through the communications system.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have no questions, but I would ask that contested document 162 be returned, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll return all the documents to you. Colonel, your testimony is now over as you have answered all the questions put to you by the Prosecution, the Defence, and the Judges. We wish to thank you for coming to The Hague, and we wish you a safe journey home with best wishes for your retirement. And I will ask the usher to be kind enough to escort you out unless Mr. Mundis has something to say first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I could, Mr. President. It might be a rather unique situation because the witness will be most likely coming back as a Defence witness. Although he's obviously taken the oath, the Prosecution would have no objection at this point with the Defence communicating with him. In effect, he can be considered released. I just want to put that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite. As I was just saying, your testimony is now over. You can contact who you wish, of course the Defence included. So there's no problem. Perhaps we will have the pleasure of seeing you again sometime in the future, but that doesn't depend on us. I wish you a safe journey home, and I will ask the usher to be kind enough to escort you out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, I give you the floor to tell us what the scheduling is for Thursday and Friday and where we stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would ask that we go into private session for just a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please. Mr. Registrar, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, I declare the end of today's hearing, as we have completed the testimony of this witness. Tomorrow's hearing will begin at 11.00 instead of at 9.00 a.m., and I invite all the participants to come back here tomorrow at 11.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
